prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There is only one data point. The starting architecture collapsed to DONE on every step: training episode length fell to 1.0 by 50% of training, and dev success was 0. A random placement usually earns a negative reward, while DONE earns 0. With normalised advantages, PPO quickly learns to stop before it ever finds the positive placements (bricks that fill missing cells at the landing layer). So the problem looks like exploration and policy collapse, not network capacity. My guesses at the fix are:
- more entropy;
- fewer PPO epochs, which buys more samples and gives gentler updates;
- a lower learning rate;
- damping how fast the DONE logit can grow.

The network only needs per-column comparisons of build height against the missing layers, plus some local context, so a small network should be enough. This round tests the recipe alone on the starting network, then the recipe plus damping of the DONE logit, then a 1-epoch recipe with more samples on a somewhat deeper network.

### Round 2
All four trials, including the baseline, collapsed straight to DONE. Neither recipe changes nor damping the DONE logit helped. The untrained traces show why: the action's column is mirrored. For example, '1x1 at col 2' filled col 5, and '1x2 at col 6' filled cols 0 and 1. Rows are not affected. So the brick actually covers columns X-dx-x to X-1-x. A translation-equivariant conv head scores the anchor using features at the wrong place, so it cannot learn which placements fill missing cells. Most placements then score below DONE's 0 reward, and DONE wins. The target heights the agent observes match the design, so the observation looks correct. The fix is architectural: re-index the placement logits so each one reads features from the cells the brick will actually fill. That is a flip after the learned layers, which the rules allow. One candidate tests the plain fix and one adds capacity. The third adds a general head that can pick any axis mirror, as a hedge in case other worlds remap actions differently.

### Round 3
This world mirrors the x-axis: placing at action column x fills cells X-dx-x to X-1-x. Every head that assumed no mirror collapsed to DONE (0.000). With the explicit x-flip, r2c1 reached 0.65 (seeds 0.56 and 0.75). The four-orientation head that had to learn the flip got 0.48, and the deeper r2c2 got 0.35. That r2c2 run also changed the recipe (2 epochs, gamma 0.97), so its result does not test either change cleanly. r2c1's training success was still rising at the end (0.28 at 75%, 0.46 at 100%), so it may be short of samples. Its remaining mistakes are about order and layers: it places a cell on the wrong layer, buries cells under a stack, or stops before finishing. This round tests three things against r2c1: more samples through fewer epochs, a longer credit horizon, and a head that reasons about which layer a brick lands on.

### Round 4
Every trial without the x-mirrored footprint head collapsed to an immediate DONE and scored 0. With the mirror, the task is learnable. The biggest gain so far came from more samples: dropping from 4 PPO epochs to 2 roughly doubled the samples and moved dev success from 0.65 to 0.90 (seeds 0.94 and 0.86), well beyond the ~0.2 seed spread. A longer credit horizon (0.62), landing-layer attention (0.59), a deeper dilated net (0.35) and the orientation-agnostic head (0.48) all scored at or below the mirrored baseline. r3c1's training success levelled off near 0.87 from 75% of training onward, and its dev IoU is 0.99, so the remaining failures are small ordering or completion errors. For the last round I keep the r3c1 network. I test 1 PPO epoch (about 400k samples), 1 epoch with smaller minibatches (more gradient steps), and a wider trunk at 1 epoch, which keeps about r3c1's sample count and tests whether capacity is the limit.

## Trial it ended with
name: Mirrored head, 1 epoch, 64 minibatches
hypothesis: Same network as r3c1, with 1 PPO epoch (about 400k samples) and 64 minibatches of 64 samples each. That doubles the gradient steps per update, which offsets the loss of the second epoch while every sample is still seen only once. Fresh data and more optimiser steps should together beat r3c1. Refuted if mean dev success is at or below 0.90, or clearly below the plain 1-epoch candidate.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).
